chapters.title: A Yogi and a Bhogi
chapters.subtitle: An inward path. A life turned toward the world.
paragraphs: Tridib Nandy begins with a familiar title: Autobiography of a Yogi. Then he changes a word. His story will be Autobiography of a Bhogi. In his telling, the bhogi is the indulgent man—the one drawn into the pleasures and experiences of life.

Yet his premise holds the two together. A life, he says, asks us to be both a yogi and a bhogi. The tension between them becomes the starting point of this book: the pull inward, and the invitation of the world outside.
These first recollections open a story still being told. They offer its central question: how might a life make room for both?

chapters.title: The inheritance
chapters.subtitle: Ancestors who were yogis. A balance of his own.
paragraphs: Tridib describes his ancestors as yogis. He describes the family into which he was born as pious. These are the roots he names at the beginning of his story.

Against that background, he places himself with a mischievous sense of balance: in this life, he has come as a bhogi. His description carries both an awareness of what came before him and the promise of a life lived in his own way.
The family stories themselves are still to come. For now, this is the thread he gives us: yogi ancestors, and a descendant exploring the other side of the balance.

chapters.title: The boy at the window
chapters.subtitle: Music, mischief, and a world beyond the classroom.
paragraphs: In Tridib’s account of his childhood, piety and mischief share the same beginning. He remembers himself as a very naughty child, known for his mischievousness at school.
Music and sports held his interest. In the classroom, his attention wandered to the window: to birds and their sounds, to trees, to the sky. The world outside drew his eye while the teachers taught.
It is a small scene with which to open a life: a child at a window, listening to something beyond the lesson. The fuller recollections will follow; the birds are already here.
